units.text: Today, separate two controls that happen to share a name. The production A P I stage points to a deployed configuration: the routes and integration settings the client actually reaches.

The Lambda alias is a different pointer. Here it sends eighty percent to one published function version and twenty percent to another. Changing those weights doesn't change which A P I deployment the stage serves.

If you're changing a route, look at the A P I stage. If you're testing a new function version behind the same integration, adjust its alias. An A P I canary has separate settings; don't use the two percentages interchangeably.

Watch a buffered REST request pass three gates. A P I Gateway accepts a payload up to ten megabytes, but a synchronous buffered Lambda invocation has a smaller six-megabyte payload limit in each direction. A request can clear the gateway size check and still be too big for its integration.

The middle gate is time, not size. The usual REST integration ceiling is twenty-nine seconds. Regional and private REST APIs can request a higher quota, which may trade off against the account's regional throttle quota.

Need to start returning results sooner? A supported REST proxy integration can stream its response for up to fifteen minutes, subject to idle limits. That changes the outbound response; it does not let the client stream an oversized request in.

The browser asks the A P I for upload permission first, not for the file transfer itself. The signing function checks who can upload and signs a short-lived U R L for the intended object key and method.

The browser receives that U R L and sends the bytes straight to S three. Treat the U R L as a bearer capability: keep it short-lived and don't expose it. The A P I and function don't carry the object bytes.

S three is where the upload lands. Verify the expected object, including its checksum where required, before calling the operation complete. The object-created event can then start processing independently.

Let's choose an endpoint by the client's path. An internet client using edge-optimized REST enters the managed CloudFront edge, then reaches the A P I's Region. A nearby edge does not give the application a second regional backend.
A Regional A P I gives the client a direct public regional endpoint. If you want to control your own CloudFront distribution and its behavior, that's a separate decision you can make here.

For a private REST A P I, the private client uses an execute-api interface endpoint in the V P C. That gets traffic to the service privately; endpoint policy, A P I resource policy and configured method authorization still govern access.

For the internal client, first confirm it can resolve and reach the execute-api endpoint over H T T P S. The security group controls network access, and the endpoint policy can constrain which permitted private APIs the caller reaches.

Reaching the endpoint isn't the same as being allowed into the A P I. Its resource policy can limit the approved endpoint or V P C, and method authorization checks the caller as configured. Only after the applicable checks pass can the request reach the integration.

A public A P I can have a private backend. The client still calls the public A P I Gateway endpoint, but A P I Gateway reaches the private load balancer through a V P C link. Current REST V P C links version two can target compatible application or network load balancers.

Compare the second path: an internal client goes through the execute-api interface endpoint to a private REST A P I. Choose this if the client-facing endpoint must be private. A V P C link by itself does not make the client entry private.
Check the backend route, listener, network rules and expected path mapping independently. Being able to reach the A P I doesn't prove that A P I Gateway can reach its target.

Let's keep one tenant's response from becoming another tenant's cache hit. After authorizing the request, partition a safely cacheable response by the tenant, resource and every variant that changes the result.

A shared key can return the wrong cached response without asking the backend again. Test with two authorized tenants requesting the same route. Use the cache lifetime for freshness, never as a substitute for isolating access. If safe partitioning isn't possible, don't cache the private response.

A signed I A M request, an appropriate Cog neato or J W T authorizer, or a Lambda authorizer can identify a caller, depending on A P I type. H T T P APIs support J W T authorizers; REST APIs have a Cog neato user-pool authorizer option.

Now check the record itself. A valid token tells you who the caller is; the application checks whether that caller can see this tenant's record. Passing gateway authentication shouldn't grant access to every record.
Route Fifty-Three locates the A P I's custom domain, and the certificate supports H T T P S. An encrypted connection protects the exchange, but doesn't authorize the caller.

At A P I Gateway, check the REST resource policy and method authorization for the caller. Then check whether the integration has permission to invoke Lambda. A caller can pass the first checks and still get an integration failure if backend permission is missing.

A browser can send an OPTIONS preflight before a cross-origin call. The A P I supplies the permitted origin and other headers, and the browser decides whether the page may read the response. Credentialed browser access needs an explicit origin, not a wildcard.

A command-line client isn't governed by browser cores checks. It still has to pass real A P I authorization. That matters because a request can reach the backend even when the browser won't expose its response to the page.
The REST A P I key identifies a client for usage-plan metering and best-effort throttles and quotas. Those limits aren't hard spending caps, and a leaked key is not proof of identity.

Keep I A M, a supported user-pool authorizer, or a Lambda authorizer in charge of access. If the client receives a four twenty-nine, check the relevant throttle and use bounded backoff for retryable operations rather than treating the key as an access credential.

Let's use an A P I error to decide where to look first. Four hundred suggests input; four oh one or four oh three points toward authentication, policy or another access check. Four twenty-nine tells you to investigate throttling, not automatically blame the function.

A five oh two can point to a failed or malformed integration response. A five oh three suggests unavailability; a five oh four may mean the integration didn't answer in time. None of those codes proves whether the backend performed the requested work.
Use the request I D to line up access logs, integration status and Lambda metrics. Confirm what actually happened before changing code or retrying a write; use idempotency where a retry is safe.
Gateway latency describes the complete time A P I Gateway spent on the request. If that rises but integration latency does not, investigate the work outside the backend span.

Integration latency begins when A P I Gateway sends the request to the backend and ends when it receives the response. If both metrics rise together for the same stage, route and time window, start by investigating that integration path.

Use a comparable statistic and look up representative requests in access logs. Where supported, execution logs and traces can separate gateway work from backend work. Keep sensitive request data out of logs.

We'll follow a WebSocket connection from admission to cleanup. The connect route runs during the handshake. The application can record the connection I D against the signed-in user; A P I Gateway doesn't automatically create that application state in Dynamo D B.

Once connected, the chosen message route handles a message, or the default route handles it when no configured route matches. Disconnect can help clean up the saved entry, but it is best effort. An I D in the database doesn't prove the connection is still active.

When the connection drops, reconnect and restore subscriptions as needed. Don't assume a handler's normal return becomes a frame on the socket; a route response must be configured if that's the behavior you expect.

For an independent push, the backend sends a signed H T T P S request to the stage's management endpoint with the intended connection I D. It uses permission to manage connections, and the gateway delivers to the client on the already-open socket.

Check the callback endpoint, the signing identity and the connection I D. If the service returns Gone for a previously established connection, treat that I D as stale and clean up the mapping instead of retrying indefinitely. For a live connection, verify that the expected client actually receives the message.
